title: At the Market
subtitle: Four scenes at the farmers' market
review: Written by Claude: check the English lines, the notes and the questions. No Burmese yet.
intro: A shopping list that comes home slightly edited, a peach tested to destruction, a bargain that saves nothing and a stall that only takes cash: four short scenes between Emma and Lucas. Listen for the amounts, the prices, and what you say when it is time to pay.

lines.text: So, did you go to the market?
Yes. Everything's in the basket.
A pound of tomatoes?
lines.note: A pound of…: we say the amount, then of, then the food.

lines.text: A pound. Nice and ripe.
lines.note: Nice and ripe = pleasantly ripe. Ripe: ready to eat.

lines.text: A bunch of parsley?
lines.note: A bunch: herbs, flowers or bananas tied or growing together.

lines.text: Cilantro. Same thing.
lines.note: Same thing = it's the same. Cilantro is the American word; in Britain it's coriander.

lines.text: It's not the same thing at all. And the piece of cheddar?
lines.note: Not… at all: a strong no.

lines.text: There's a piece left.
lines.note: Left: still there, not eaten or used.

lines.text: What do you mean, "left"?
lines.note: What do you mean? asks for an explanation.

lines.text: I tried it before I bought it. And a little after.
lines.note: Try food = taste it to see if you like it.

lines.text: Are these peaches ripe?
Stop touching everything.
lines.note: Stop + verb-ing: stop touching, stop talking.

lines.text: I'm just checking. This one's hard. So is this one.
lines.note: So is this one = this one is hard too.

lines.text: Is it for today or for tomorrow?
For tonight.
Then you need a really ripe one.
lines.note: One replaces the noun: a ripe one = a ripe peach.

lines.text: This one's soft. Very soft.
Of course it is. You've been squeezing it for five minutes.
lines.note: You've been squeezing: it started five minutes ago and has not stopped. Squeeze: press with your fingers.

lines.text: So it's ripe.
It's bruised. And now it's ours.
lines.note: Bruised: damaged, with a soft dark spot. Ours = it belongs to us.

lines.text: Four dollars for a basket of strawberries! That's expensive.
lines.note: Expensive: it costs a lot. The opposite is cheap.

lines.text: They're organic, local, and in season.
lines.note: In season: it is the time of year when they grow.

lines.text: You're reading the sign.
Hold on. I'm going to bargain.
lines.note: Hold on = wait. Bargain: ask the seller for a lower price.

lines.text: People don't really do that here.
lines.note: Not really = not much, not usually.

lines.text: Watch and learn. … There. Two baskets for eight dollars.
lines.note: Watch and learn: said by someone very sure of himself.

lines.text: Lucas. That's the same price.
Yes, but now we have two.
And four dollars less.
lines.note: Less: a smaller amount. The opposite is more.

lines.text: That comes to twelve fifty.
lines.note: That comes to… = the total is… Twelve fifty = $12.50.

lines.text: I'll pay by card.
lines.note: Pay by card, but pay in cash.

lines.text: He doesn't take cards. Cash only.
lines.note: He is the seller. Take cards = accept cards.

lines.text: Not even tap to pay?
lines.note: Not even: it makes the no stronger. Tap to pay: you touch the machine with your card or phone.

lines.text: Lucas. His scale is older than you are.
lines.note: A scale weighs the fruit and vegetables.

lines.text: Fine. I've got a fifty.
lines.note: A fifty = a fifty-dollar bill.

lines.text: He can't break a fifty. Do you have anything smaller?
lines.note: Break a fifty: give change for it. Anything smaller: smaller bills or coins.

lines.text: I have two dollars… and a button.
Never mind. I'll pay. You owe me twelve fifty and a button.
lines.note: Never mind = forget it. Owe: you must pay it back.

notes: Amounts take of: a pound of tomatoes, a bunch of parsley, a piece of cheese, a basket of strawberries.
One replaces a noun you have already said: this one, a ripe one.
For fruit: ripe (ready to eat), hard, soft, bruised (damaged).
Prices: four dollars for a basket, two for eight dollars. That comes to twelve fifty = the total is $12.50.
To pay: by card, in cash, tap to pay. Cash only = no cards.
He can't break a fifty = he has no change for a fifty-dollar bill.

questions.q: Lucas bought cilantro, not parsley. What does he say?
questions.why: Same thing = it's the same. Emma answers: It's not the same thing at all.

questions.q: The peach is for tonight. What does Lucas need?
questions.why: Emma says: Then you need a really ripe one.
Emma says: You've been squeezing it for five minutes.

questions.q: Lucas bargains and gets two baskets for eight dollars. How much does he save?
questions.why: One basket is four dollars, so two are eight: that's the same price.

questions.q: The seller does not take cards. How do they have to pay?
questions.why: Emma says: He doesn't take cards. Cash only.
